people.name: Flavius Josephus
people.summary: Jewish priest and general who went over to Rome in the war of 66–70 and wrote its history; our main narrative source for first-century Judea.

people.name: Philo of Alexandria
people.summary: Jewish philosopher of Alexandria, contemporary of Jesus, who read the Torah through Greek philosophy and led an embassy to the emperor Gaius.

people.name: Cornelius Tacitus
people.summary: Roman senator and historian of the early emperors; his Annals record Nero's punishment of Christians after the fire of Rome.

people.name: Suetonius
people.summary: Roman biographer and imperial secretary who wrote lives of the first twelve Caesars.

people.name: Pliny the Younger
people.summary: Roman senator and governor of Bithynia-Pontus whose letter to Trajan (Letters 10.96) is the earliest pagan description of Christian worship.

people.name: Pliny the Elder
people.summary: Roman officer and encyclopedist who died in the eruption of Vesuvius; his Natural History mentions the Essenes by the Dead Sea.

people.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
people.summary: Roman orator, lawyer and philosopher whose speeches and treatises show Roman ideas of citizenship, duty, fides and patronage.

people.name: Augustus
people.summary: First Roman emperor, adopted son of Julius Caesar; emperor when Jesus was born (Luke 2:1). His own account of his deeds survives in inscriptions.

people.name: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, tutor and adviser to Nero, brother of the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12); wrote on benefits, slavery and suffering.

people.name: Gaius (jurist)
people.summary: Second-century Roman jurist whose Institutes, a teaching manual, are the fullest surviving account of classical Roman private law.

people.name: Polybius
people.summary: Greek historian of Rome's rise to power, who described the Roman army and constitution from close observation.

people.name: Aristotle
people.summary: Greek philosopher whose Politics set out the household as master and slave, husband and wife, father and children.

people.name: Adolf Deissmann
people.summary: German New Testament scholar who used papyri and inscriptions to show that NT Greek was the everyday language of the Roman East.

entries.title: Good news (euangelion)
entries.subtitle: Imperial announcements and the gospel of the Son
entries.summary: In the Roman East *euangelion* was the word for public good news: a victory, an emperor's birth or accession. The NT uses it for the announcement that Jesus is the Son and Lord.

entries.title: Lord (kyrios)
entries.subtitle: Caesar's title and the confession 'Jesus is Lord'
entries.summary: *Kyrios* meant master, owner or ruler, and it was used of emperors in the East. In the LXX it stands for the divine name. Calling Jesus *kyrios* drew on both.

entries.title: Saviour (sōtēr)
entries.subtitle: Benefactor-kings, emperors and the Saviour from heaven
entries.summary: Hellenistic kings and Roman emperors were hailed as *sōtēr*, saviour and preserver of cities. The NT gives the title to God and to Jesus.

entries.title: Assembly (ekklēsia)
entries.subtitle: The citizens' assembly and the gathering of God's people
entries.summary: In a Greek city the *ekklēsia* was the assembly of citizens called together to decide public business. The LXX used it for Israel gathered before God. The church took the name.

entries.title: Coming (parousia)
entries.subtitle: The royal visit and the coming of the Son
entries.summary: *Parousia* means 'presence' or 'arrival'. In Hellenistic usage it was a technical term for the official visit of a king or high official to a city, marked by crowns, speeches and celebrations.

entries.title: Meeting (apantēsis)
entries.subtitle: Going out to meet a dignitary and escorting him in
entries.summary: *Apantēsis* describes going out from a city to meet an arriving dignitary and escorting him back in. The NT uses it for meeting the Lord in 1 Thess 4:17.

entries.title: Kingdom (basileia)
entries.subtitle: Caesar's empire and the reign of God
entries.summary: *Basileia* is kingship or reign more than territory. In the Greek East the emperor was often called *basileus*, king. Jesus announced the reign of God as arriving in himself.

entries.title: Adoption (huiothesia / adoptio)
entries.subtitle: Placed as a son with full rights
entries.summary: Roman adoption moved a person fully into a new family: new father, new name, new heir, old debts cancelled. Paul uses *huiothesia* for what the Father does in the Son by the Spirit.

entries.title: Father's power (patria potestas)
entries.subtitle: The Roman father's legal authority over his children
entries.summary: In Roman law a father held *potestas* over his children, and over their children, for as long as he lived: their property, marriages and in theory their lives were under his authority.

entries.title: Head of household (paterfamilias)
entries.subtitle: The householder in the parables and the Roman home
entries.summary: The *paterfamilias* was the head of a Roman household (*familia*), which included wife, children, slaves, freedmen and property. Greek *oikodespotēs*, 'master of the house', is the parables' householder.

entries.title: Patronage (patronus and cliens)
entries.subtitle: Benefactors, clients and the economy of favour
entries.summary: Roman society ran on patronage: patrons gave protection, money and access; clients gave loyalty, public support and honour. Gifts created bonds and obligations.

entries.title: Faith and faithfulness (pistis / fides)
entries.subtitle: Trust, loyalty and keeping faith
entries.summary: *Pistis* and Latin *fides* covered trust, trustworthiness and loyalty: the faith a client kept with a patron, the good faith of a treaty, the reliability of one's word.

entries.title: Grace as benefaction (charis)
entries.subtitle: Gift, favour and gratitude
entries.summary: In Greco-Roman culture *charis* was the whole circle of a gift: the favour of the giver, the gift itself and the gratitude of the receiver.

entries.title: Honour and shame
entries.subtitle: Public worth, reputation and the shame of the cross
entries.summary: Mediterranean societies measured worth by public honour: reputation granted by family, city and peers. Shame was public loss of standing.

entries.title: Citizenship (politeuma, civis Romanus)
entries.subtitle: Roman citizens, colonies and the heavenly commonwealth
entries.summary: Roman citizenship was a privileged legal status that protected its holder from flogging and summary execution. A *politeuma* was a commonwealth or citizen body, including communities living abroad.

entries.title: Appeal to Caesar (provocatio)
entries.subtitle: A citizen's right to be heard by the emperor
entries.summary: A Roman citizen facing a capital charge in the provinces could appeal to the emperor's court. Paul did so before Festus, which is how he came to Rome.

entries.title: Proconsul (anthypatos)
entries.subtitle: Governors of the senatorial provinces
entries.summary: A proconsul governed a province assigned to the senate. Acts names two: Sergius Paulus in Cyprus and Gallio in Achaia.

entries.title: Prefect and procurator (hēgemōn)
entries.subtitle: Pilate, Felix, Festus and the governors of Judea
entries.summary: After AD 6 Judea was governed by Roman equestrian officials. Pilate's title was prefect; later governors were called procurators. The NT uses the general word *hēgemōn*, governor.

entries.title: Tetrarch (tetraarchēs)
entries.subtitle: Herod Antipas, Philip and the division of Herod's kingdom
entries.summary: A tetrarch ('ruler of a quarter') was a minor dependent ruler. After Herod the Great died, Augustus divided his kingdom: Archelaus received Judea, Antipas Galilee and Perea, Philip the north-east.

entries.title: Centurion (hekatontarchēs)
entries.subtitle: Roman officers who meet Jesus and the apostles
entries.summary: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred men, and was the backbone of the Roman army. Centurions appear in the NT more favourably than almost any other group.

entries.title: Legion (legiōn)
entries.subtitle: Rome's army units and a demon's name
entries.summary: A legion was the main heavy-infantry unit of the Roman army, around five thousand citizen soldiers with supporting troops. The word became a byword for overwhelming force.

entries.title: Praetorian guard and praetorium
entries.subtitle: The emperor's guard and the governor's headquarters
entries.summary: The *praetorium* was first a general's tent, then a governor's residence. The praetorian cohorts were the emperor's guard in Rome.

entries.title: Crucifixion (stauros)
entries.subtitle: Rome's most shameful punishment
entries.summary: Crucifixion was a slow, public, humiliating execution reserved mainly for slaves, rebels and the lowest classes. Roman citizens were normally exempt.

entries.title: Charge placard (titulus)
entries.subtitle: The inscription on the cross
entries.summary: A *titulus* was a placard stating the condemned person's crime, carried before him or fixed to the cross to warn onlookers.

entries.title: Tribute and census (kēnsos, phoros)
entries.subtitle: Taxes to Caesar and the census of Quirinius
entries.summary: Provinces paid direct tribute to Rome, assessed by census. The census of Judea in AD 6 provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean; the tribute question became a test of loyalty.

entries.title: Tax collectors (telōnai, publicani)
entries.subtitle: Toll collectors and their reputation
entries.summary: Rome sold the right to collect certain taxes and tolls to contractors (*publicani*), who used local collectors. The Gospels' *telōnai* were local toll collectors, despised as collaborators and extortioners.

entries.title: Denarius (dēnarion)
entries.subtitle: The silver coin of wages and tribute
entries.summary: The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin. In the Gospels it is a day's wage for a labourer, and the coin of the tribute.

entries.title: Freedman (apeleutheros, libertus)
entries.subtitle: Former slaves and their ties to their patrons
entries.summary: A freed slave (*libertus*) became free, often a Roman citizen, but remained bound to his former master, now his patron, by duties of respect and service.

entries.title: Slavery (doulos)
entries.subtitle: Slaves, masters and the Lord who became a slave
entries.summary: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Slaves were legally property, though their conditions ranged from mines to managing estates. Many early believers were slaves.

entries.title: Ransom price (lytron)
entries.subtitle: Release of captives and slaves
entries.summary: A *lytron* was the price paid to release a prisoner of war, a slave or a pledged life. In the LXX it is used for redeeming the firstborn, land and kin.

entries.title: Manumission
entries.subtitle: Freeing slaves, and 'bought with a price'
entries.summary: Manumission was the legal freeing of a slave, by formal act, census or will. It was common in Roman society and often expected after years of service.

entries.title: Triumph (thriambeuō)
entries.subtitle: The victory procession of a Roman general
entries.summary: A Roman triumph was a sacred procession in which a victorious general rode through Rome with his army, spoils and captive enemy leaders, who were often executed at the end.

entries.title: Libation (spendō)
entries.subtitle: A poured-out drink offering
entries.summary: A libation was wine (or other liquid) poured out to a deity, both in Israel's sacrifices and in Greco-Roman household rites, banquets and public sacrifices.

entries.title: Imperial cult
entries.subtitle: Temples, priests and sacrifices for the emperor
entries.summary: In the eastern provinces cities competed to build temples to the emperor and Rome, held festivals and offered sacrifices. Emperors who died could be declared divine (*divus*) by the senate.

entries.title: Peace of Rome (pax Romana)
entries.subtitle: Augustan peace and the peace of Christ
entries.summary: Augustus' propaganda celebrated peace won by victory: the temple of Janus closed, the Altar of Augustan Peace dedicated. Peace was the fruit of Roman conquest.

entries.title: Caesar (Kaisar)
entries.subtitle: The family name that became an imperial title
entries.summary: Caesar was Julius Caesar's family name, taken by his adopted son Augustus and then used as a title by the emperors. The NT names Augustus (Luke 2:1), Tiberius (Luke 3:1) and Claudius (Acts 11:28; 18:2), and Nero is 'Caesar' in Acts 25.

entries.title: Herodians (Hērōdianoi)
entries.subtitle: Supporters of the Herodian house
entries.summary: The Herodians appear only in Mark and Matthew, plotting with Pharisees against Jesus and asking the tribute question. They were probably supporters of Herod Antipas and the Herodian family's rule under Rome.

entries.title: Sanhedrin (synedrion)
entries.subtitle: The Jerusalem council
entries.summary: *Synedrion* means council. In Jerusalem the high priest presided over a council of chief priests, elders and scribes, which handled religious and civic matters under Roman oversight.

entries.title: Synagogue (synagōgē)
entries.subtitle: The Jewish assembly for reading and prayer
entries.summary: *Synagōgē* means gathering. By the first century Jews gathered every sabbath in Judea and throughout the diaspora to read and explain the Law and Prophets, in buildings also called *proseuchē*, 'place of prayer'.

entries.title: Pharisees (Pharisaioi)
entries.subtitle: Lay experts in the Law and its traditions
entries.summary: The Pharisees were a popular movement devoted to precise observance of the Law and the 'traditions of the fathers'. They believed in resurrection and in angels and spirits, and they had wide influence among ordinary people.

entries.title: Sadducees (Saddoukaioi)
entries.subtitle: The priestly aristocracy
entries.summary: The Sadducees were a party of the priestly and wealthy elite, closely tied to the temple and to cooperation with Rome. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and denied resurrection.

entries.title: Essenes
entries.subtitle: A disciplined Jewish community not named in the NT
entries.summary: The Essenes were a strict Jewish movement described by Josephus, Philo and Pliny the Elder, living in communities with shared property, ritual washings, communal meals and rigorous discipline. They are not mentioned in the NT.

entries.title: Zealots (zēlōtai)
entries.subtitle: Zeal for the Law and armed resistance
entries.summary: 'Zealot' could describe anyone zealous for God and the Law (Acts 21:20; Gal 1:14). Josephus uses it as the name of a revolutionary faction during the war of 66–70. One of the Twelve was 'Simon the Zealot'.

entries.title: Samaritans (Samaritai)
entries.subtitle: Israel's estranged cousins
entries.summary: The Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee, worshipped the God of Israel, accepted the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. Relations with Jews were hostile.

entries.title: Diaspora (diaspora)
entries.subtitle: Jews scattered among the nations
entries.summary: By the first century most Jews lived outside the land of Israel, in large communities in Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, Asia Minor, Babylonia and elsewhere.

entries.title: God-fearers (phoboumenoi / sebomenoi ton theon)
entries.subtitle: Gentiles attached to the synagogue
entries.summary: Acts describes Gentiles who worshipped Israel's God and attended synagogue without becoming full converts: 'those who fear God' and 'devout' or 'worshipping' Greeks.

entries.title: Proselyte (prosēlytos)
entries.subtitle: A Gentile convert to Judaism
entries.summary: A proselyte was a Gentile who fully converted to Judaism, for men including circumcision, and took on the Law. In the LXX *prosēlytos* translates *ger*, the resident foreigner.

entries.title: Jubilee and release of debts (aphesis)
entries.subtitle: Sabbath years, debt and the year of the Lord's favour
entries.summary: The Torah commanded release of debts every seventh year and, every fiftieth, a Jubilee in which land returned to its families and slaves went free. The LXX calls it *aphesis*, release, the word later used for forgiveness.

entries.title: Gymnasium and ephebeia
entries.subtitle: Greek education, athletic training and identity
entries.summary: The gymnasium was the centre of Greek civic education, where young citizens (*ephebes*) trained in athletics and learning. Membership marked one as Greek.

entries.title: Banquet and symposium
entries.subtitle: Reclining at table, rank and the Lord's supper
entries.summary: Greco-Roman meals for guests followed set customs: guests reclined on couches by rank, the meal (*deipnon*) was followed by drinking and conversation (*symposion*), and the seating displayed honour.

entries.title: Hospitality (philoxenia)
entries.subtitle: Welcoming strangers
entries.summary: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty across the ancient Mediterranean. Travelling believers depended on it, and the early church made it a mark of leaders and members alike.

entries.title: Household codes
entries.subtitle: Instructions for husbands, wives, parents, children, masters and slaves
entries.summary: Several NT letters contain 'household codes', paired instructions for the members of a household. The form follows a long Greek tradition of discussing household management.

entries.title: Letters (epistolē)
entries.subtitle: Ancient epistolary conventions
entries.summary: Greek letters followed a fixed form: sender to recipient, greeting (*chairein*), thanksgiving or health wish, body, closing greetings and farewell. Letters were carried by trusted messengers who often read and explained them.

entries.title: Reconciliation (katallagē)
entries.subtitle: Diplomacy, ambassadors and the end of hostility
entries.summary: *Katallassō* meant to change enmity into friendship: between warring states, estranged spouses or quarrelling parties. Ambassadors (*presbeis*) negotiated such reconciliations.

entries.title: Christians (Christianoi)
entries.subtitle: A Latin-style name and Roman suspicion
entries.summary: The name 'Christians' is formed like Latin party names (*Caesariani*, *Pompeiani*): partisans of Christus. It first appears at Antioch (Acts 11:26).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/euangelion
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In 9 BC the province of Asia adopted a new calendar starting the year on Augustus' birthday. The decree, found at Priene, says that the birthday of 'the god' was for the world the beginning of the good news (*euangelia*) that came through him, and calls him a saviour who ended war.

Josephus uses the same language for Vespasian's accession in AD 69: cities celebrated the good news (*euangelia*) with sacrifices (Jewish War 4.618, 4.656).

The word also had a Jewish background: Isa 52:7 and 61:1 (LXX) use the verb *euangelizō* for the herald who announces that 'your God reigns'.

citations.ref: Priene Calendar Inscription (OGIS 458), lines on Augustus' birthday

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/euangelion
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Mark opens with 'the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God' (Mark 1:1), the kind of line a city would carve for an emperor. But this herald announces a different kind of reign: a Son who reveals the Father by healing, eating with outsiders and giving his life away.

The gospel is first news about a person and a relationship, not a set of terms. Paul's summary in Rom 1:3–4 is about who Jesus is: David's son, declared Son of God in power by the resurrection. The good news is that the Father's kingdom has arrived in his Son and that all are invited home.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/euangelion
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body:
**How anti-imperial is Paul's gospel?** Many scholars hold that Paul's use of *euangelion*, *kyrios*, *sōtēr* and *parousia* deliberately echoes and challenges imperial propaganda, so that 'Jesus is Lord' implies 'Caesar is not'.

Others reply that these words were ordinary Greek, that Paul's main background is Isaiah and the Psalms, and that he rarely mentions Rome directly (and in Rom 13:1–7 counsels respect for authorities). They warn against reading coded resistance into every term.

A middle view: Paul's primary source is Israel's Scriptures, but his hearers in Roman cities could not miss the overlap, and the gospel relativised every rival claim to lordship without being a political programme.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/kyrios
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
*Kyrios* was the ordinary word for a slave's master or a property owner. In the Greek East it was also used of rulers: Festus calls Nero 'my lord' (*tō kyriō*) in Acts 25:26.

Roman emperors handled the title differently. Suetonius says Augustus recoiled from being called *dominus* as an insult (Augustus 53), while Domitian liked to be styled 'our lord and god' (Domitian 13). Pliny addresses Trajan as *domine* throughout Book 10 of his letters.

A generation later the police captain urged the aged Polycarp: 'What harm is there in saying Lord Caesar and offering incense?' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 8.2).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/kyrios
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
'Jesus is Lord' (Rom 10:9) is a confession of trust and belonging, not only of rank. In the LXX *kyrios* renders the name of Israel's God, so Paul can place Jesus inside the Shema: 'one God, the Father ... and one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 8:6).

This Lord does not rule by domination. Phil 2:6–11 says he received the name above every name because he emptied himself and took the form of a slave. The world's lords 'lord it over' others (Mark 10:42); the true Lord kneels to wash feet. Lordship, seen in Jesus, is the Father's self-giving love on the throne.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/soter
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Greek cities honoured kings and generals who rescued or endowed them as *sōtēr*, often alongside *euergetēs* (benefactor). The Priene decree for Augustus (9 BC) praises providence for sending a saviour who put an end to war and set all things in order.

The Samaritans' confession that Jesus is 'the Saviour of the world' (John 4:42) and the angel's 'a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord' (Luke 2:11), announced in the reign of Augustus, use the same register.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/soter
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
In the NT salvation is rescue into life with God: healing, deliverance from the powers, return from exile, adoption. The Saviour is the one who comes to where we are and brings us home (Luke 19:10).

Phil 3:20 is pointed for a Roman colony: 'our citizenship is in heaven, from where we await a Saviour'. The Saviour the Philippians wait for does not arrive with legions but with the power to transform 'our lowly body' into the likeness of his own. The emperor saved cities by force; Jesus saves by union with his own risen life.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/ekklesia
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In Greek cities the *ekklēsia* was the formal meeting of the citizen body. Acts 19 shows the word in this civic sense: the Ephesian riot is a disorderly *ekklēsia* (Acts 19:32), and the town clerk tells the crowd to bring complaints to 'the lawful assembly' (*ennomos ekklēsia*, 19:39), then dismisses it (19:41).

In the LXX *ekklēsia* often translates Hebrew *qahal*, the assembly of Israel (for example Deut 9:10, 'the day of the assembly' at Sinai).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/ekklesia
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
When Paul writes 'to the *ekklēsia* of the Thessalonians in God the Father' (1 Thess 1:1), he names a gathering whose life is located in a Father and a Son. Slaves, women and foreigners, who had no vote in the city assembly, belong fully in this one.

The church is not a club or a department of religion. It is a new public: a family-assembly gathered by the Father, where the Son's way of life is practised in the open as a sign of the kingdom to the city.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/parousia
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
*Parousia* can be ordinary: Paul is cheered by 'the coming of Titus' (2 Cor 7:6), and his opponents say his bodily presence is weak (2 Cor 10:10).

In papyri and inscriptions it also names the formal visit of a ruler. Cities prepared roads and gifts, struck coins and sometimes counted a new era from the visit. The Latin equivalent was *adventus*.

citations.ref: Light from the Ancient East (on parousia and adventus)

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/parousia
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The NT uses the language of a royal visit for the coming of Jesus, but the King who comes is the one who already came in humility and lives among his people by the Spirit. His 'presence' is the goal of history: God's family gathered and transformed (1 Cor 15:23).

On a postmillennial reading the kingdom grows now, like yeast through dough, and the final *parousia* crowns a world already being filled with the knowledge of the Lord. It is not an escape from a failed earth but the King's arrival to complete what he began.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/parousia
blocks.body: Deissmann argued from papyri and inscriptions that *parousia* was a technical term for the visit of a king or emperor, with its own ceremonies, coinage and sometimes a new era-reckoning, and that early Christians heard Christ's coming against this background.

citations.ref: Light from the Ancient East (on parousia)

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/parousia
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **Which coming?** In Matt 24:3 the disciples ask about the temple's destruction and 'your coming'. Partial-preterist readers hold that much of Matt 24:4–34 was fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 ('this generation', 24:34), while 1 Cor 15:23 and 1 Thess 4:15 look to a final bodily return. Futurist readers apply most of Matt 24 to the end of history. Others see the two horizons deliberately overlapping.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/apantesis
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
When an important visitor approached, leading citizens went out along the road to meet him and accompany him into the city. Acts 28:15 shows believers doing exactly this for Paul: they came from Rome as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns 'to meet us' (*eis apantēsin*).

In the parable of the bridesmaids the cry is 'Go out to meet him' (Matt 25:6), and the bridesmaids then go in with the bridegroom.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/apantesis
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
In 1 Thess 4:17 believers are 'caught up ... to meet (*eis apantēsin*) the Lord in the air'. If Paul uses the word in its customary sense, the picture is not of the church leaving the earth but of the welcoming party going out to greet the coming King and escorting him back to the world he is renewing.

The hope is reunion and welcome: 'so we will always be with the Lord'. Paul gives it as comfort for grieving families (4:18), not as a timetable.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/apantesis
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Whether *apantēsis* carries its technical civic sense in 1 Thess 4:17 is debated. Many commentators accept the escort reading and conclude that believers return with the Lord to earth. Others note that the word can simply mean 'meeting' and that Paul does not say what happens next. Pre-tribulation rapture readings, in which the church is taken away to heaven before a later return, are a nineteenth-century development and a minority among NT scholars.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/basileia
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Augustus presented his rule as the restoration of the republic: in Res Gestae 34 he says he transferred the state to the senate and people and was given the name Augustus. In practice he held supreme power, and Greek-speaking subjects called the emperor *basileus* (compare 1 Pet 2:13, 17).

The accusation in Thessalonica was that Christians acted 'against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus' (Acts 17:7). At Jesus' trial the chief priests say, 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19:15).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/basileia
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The kingdom of God is the Father's reign of love made present in the Son. It comes not by legions but like a mustard seed and like yeast (Matt 13:31–33): small, hidden, unstoppable.

'My kingdom is not of (*ek*) this world' (John 18:36) speaks of its source, not its location. It does not draw its power from the sword, yet it is for this world: 'your will be done on earth as in heaven'. On a postmillennial reading the stone of Dan 2:35 grows to fill the earth as the gospel spreads, and Rev 11:15 is the destiny of history: the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/huiothesia
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Roman law distinguished *adoptio* (taking a person who was under another father's power) from *adrogatio* (taking a person who was legally independent, together with his household and property). Gaius sets out both and explains that the adopted person passes into the power (*potestas*) of the adoptive father (Gaius, Institutes 1.97–107).

Adoption was common among the elite and was central to imperial succession. Julius Caesar adopted his great-nephew Octavius in his will (Suetonius, Julius 83), and Augustus later adopted Tiberius (Suetonius, Tiberius 21). The adopted son took the father's name and inheritance.

The Torah has no formal adoption law, and the word *huiothesia* does not occur in the LXX.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/huiothesia
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Adoption is the heart of the relational gospel. The eternal Son shares his sonship: 'God sent his Son ... so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying Abba, Father!' (Gal 4:4–6).

This is not a legal fiction filed in heaven. The Spirit makes it real inside us; we call God what Jesus calls him. Eph 1:5 says the Father planned it 'before the foundation of the world', so adoption is not a rescue plan after the fall but the purpose of creation. And Rom 8:23 says it will be complete when our bodies are raised: the whole person brought into the Father's house.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/huiothesia
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **Roman or Jewish background?** Many read *huiothesia* against Roman adoption, since Paul wrote to Romans, Galatians and Ephesians in Roman cities and the word is a legal term. Others stress the Jewish story: Israel as God's son (Exod 4:22; Rom 9:4), the Davidic promise 'I will be his father' (2 Sam 7:14), and the exodus from slavery that frames Gal 4 and Rom 8. Both are likely in view: the Roman term names the Jewish hope.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/huiothesia
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
**How the legal reading arose.** In Reformed theology adoption became a step in the order of salvation following justification, defined as a judicial act (Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 12, 'Of Adoption'). The emphasis fell on change of status before a judge.

Relational authors do not deny the change of status but put it inside the Father's love and the Son's own sonship: we are adopted 'in him' (Eph 1:5), and the Spirit of the Son is given so that the relationship is lived, not only declared.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/patria-potestas
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Gaius calls the power of fathers over their children a right peculiar to Roman citizens, adding that hardly any other people held such power over their sons (Institutes 1.55). A son, however old, owned nothing in his own right while his father lived, unless he was emancipated.

Gal 4:1–2 assumes a related arrangement: the heir, while a minor, is no different from a slave and is under guardians (*epitropoi*) and managers until the date set by the father.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/patria-potestas
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus' picture of the Father cuts across the Roman model. In the parable of the lost son (Luke 15) the father lets the son go, runs to meet him, and restores him before any terms are set. Power is used to give and to restore, not to control.

Paul writes 'the Father, from whom every family (*patria*) in heaven and on earth is named' (Eph 3:14–15). Human fatherhood is measured by God's, not the other way round. When we read 'father' in the NT we should hear Jesus' Abba, not Roman *potestas*.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/paterfamilias
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Roman law divided persons into those 'in their own power' (*sui iuris*) and those 'in the power of another' (*alieni iuris*); the *paterfamilias* was the one in his own power, and the rest of the household was under him (Gaius, Institutes 1.48–55).

The household was also the basic unit of economy and religion: the head led household worship and was responsible for its members. When a householder was baptized, his household often followed (Acts 16:15, 31–34; 1 Cor 1:16).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/paterfamilias
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus often casts God as a householder, but a surprising one: he pays the last hired the same as the first (Matt 20:1–16) and fills his banquet with the poor and disabled from the streets (Luke 14:21). The household of God is defined by the Father's generosity.

The early churches met in households, and the household became the place where a new family was formed across lines of rank. 'You are no longer strangers ... but members of the household of God' (Eph 2:19).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/patronage
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Seneca's treatise On Benefits is a long reflection on giving and receiving favour. He explains the three Graces dancing hand in hand as the circle of a benefit passing from giver to receiver and back again (On Benefits 1.3).

Cicero observes that proud men think it like death to have accepted a patron's protection or to be called clients (On Duties 2.69), which shows how status-laden the relationship was.

In the NT the centurion at Capernaum is a patron of the local Jews: 'he loves our nation and built us our synagogue' (Luke 7:5). Phoebe is called a *prostatis*, patroness, of many including Paul (Rom 16:2).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/patronage
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Patronage gives the NT its grammar of grace. God is the great Benefactor whose gifts come first, without regard to worth, and who creates a relationship of gratitude and faithfulness.

But Jesus turns the system inside out: 'The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority are called benefactors. Not so with you' (Luke 22:25–26). The greatest becomes the servant. The Father does not give to secure clients; he gives to make children. Gratitude in the NT is the response of sons and daughters, not the repayment of a debt.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pistis-fides
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Cicero calls good faith (*fides*) the foundation of justice: constancy and truthfulness in what is said and agreed (On Duties 1.23). Fides was even honoured as a goddess with a temple on the Capitol.

In patronage and diplomacy, *fides* named the reliability that bound the two parties: a people that surrendered into Rome's *fides* placed itself under Rome's protection. In Greek, *pistis* similarly covered both the trust given and the faithfulness shown.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pistis-fides
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
NT faith is relational: trust in a person who has proved faithful, and loyalty in return. Paul's 'obedience of faith' (Rom 1:5) is allegiance that comes from trust, not a separate work.

The Father's faithfulness comes first and is seen in the faithfulness of Jesus, who trusted the Father all the way to the cross. We are drawn into that trust: 'I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me' (Gal 2:20, KJV). Faith is sharing in the Son's own life of trust toward the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pistis-fides
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **'Faith in Christ' or 'faithfulness of Christ'?** The Greek phrase *pistis Christou* (Rom 3:22; Gal 2:16, 20; Phil 3:9) can be read as an objective genitive, 'faith in Christ', or a subjective genitive, 'the faith(fulness) of Christ'. The KJV often has 'faith of Christ'; most modern versions have 'faith in Christ'. Scholars remain divided, and the choice shapes whether the stress falls on our believing or on Christ's own faithfulness in which we share.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/charis
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Benefactors (*euergetai*) endowed buildings, games and grain for cities and were honoured with inscriptions and statues; the giver's *charis* called for the receiver's *charis* in return. Seneca's picture of the three Graces with linked hands describes this circle of giving, receiving and returning (On Benefits 1.3).

Gifts were usually given to worthy recipients who could return honour. Seneca discusses at length whom one should benefit (On Benefits, book 1 and following).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/charis
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
God's *charis* breaks the rule that gifts go to the worthy: 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us' (Rom 5:8). Yet grace still makes a circle. It creates a relationship in which the receiver responds with love, trust and generosity to others (2 Cor 8–9).

Grace is not a substance or a ledger credit but the Father's self-giving in the Son. 'You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9). We are saved by grace for the good works he prepared (Eph 2:8–10): the circle of the Graces, centred on God.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/honour-shame
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Seating at banquets, places in procession, titles in inscriptions and the regard of one's peers all marked honour. Jesus' advice not to take the place of honour at a wedding feast (Luke 14:8–10) assumes everyone watched where guests reclined.

Crucifixion was designed to strip a person of every honour. Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross 'despising the shame' (Heb 12:2).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/honour-shame
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The gospel reorders honour. The Son, who shared the Father's glory, took the most shameful place there was (Phil 2:5–11), and the Father honoured him with the name above every name. In him the shamed are given a seat at the table.

This helps read sin and salvation relationally: sin dishonours the Father and shames us; salvation is the Father covering our shame, as the father in Luke 15 covers his son with the best robe before the village can mock him. 'Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame' (Rom 10:11).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/citizenship
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Being a Roman citizen exempted a person from degrading punishments. Cicero's prosecution of Verres turns on the scandal that a man crying 'I am a Roman citizen' (*civis Romanus sum*) was flogged and crucified in Sicily (Against Verres 2.5.162–170).

Acts reflects the same protections. At Philippi, a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), the magistrates are alarmed to learn they have beaten Roman citizens uncondemned (16:37–38). In Jerusalem the tribune halts a flogging when Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge a Roman uncondemned; the tribune bought his citizenship, but Paul was born a citizen (22:25–29).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/citizenship
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul tells the Philippians, proud citizens of a Roman colony, 'our citizenship (*politeuma*) is in heaven' (Phil 3:20) and 'live as citizens (*politeuesthe*) worthy of the gospel' (1:27). The church is a colony of heaven: an outpost of the Father's commonwealth living its customs in the middle of the empire.

Gentiles once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel' are now 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God' (Eph 2:12, 19). Citizenship and family belong together: we belong to a city because we have been made children of its Father.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/provocatio
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Paul's words before Festus, 'I appeal to Caesar' (Acts 25:11), use a citizen's right; Festus confers with his council and replies, 'To Caesar you shall go' (25:12). Agrippa later says Paul could have been released if he had not appealed (26:32).

Pliny, as governor of Bithynia about AD 112, says he sent accused Christians who were Roman citizens to Rome for trial, while executing non-citizens who persisted (Letters 10.96).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/provocatio
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul uses Roman law without trusting in it. His appeal serves the mission the risen Lord had promised: 'you must testify also in Rome' (Acts 23:11). The empire's legal machinery becomes the road by which the gospel reaches its capital.

The story invites a relational reading of authority: the believer can honour legitimate structures and use them for the good of others, while knowing that his life is held by a different King.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/proconsul
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Augustus kept the militarily important provinces for himself and let the senate assign the others to proconsuls chosen by lot (Suetonius, Augustus 47). Cyprus, Achaia and Asia were senatorial provinces, and Acts correctly calls their governors proconsuls (Acts 13:7; 18:12; 19:38).

An inscription found at Delphi preserves a letter of the emperor Claudius that names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia. It is one of the main anchors for dating Paul's stay in Corinth to about AD 50–52. Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/proconsul
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Sergius Paulus is called 'an intelligent man' who 'believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord' (Acts 13:7, 12). Gallio refuses to judge a Jewish dispute about words and names (18:14–15). Luke shows the gospel meeting Roman power both as a summons to faith and as a matter the state is not competent to judge.

The Father's message is for governors as well as slaves; neither rank brings someone nearer to him or puts him out of reach.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/prefect-procurator
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
A stone found in the theatre at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 names Pontius Pilate as *praefectus Iudaeae*, prefect of Judea. Tacitus, writing later, calls him procurator (Annals 15.44), the title used for governors after Claudius.

Josephus describes clashes under Pilate: the night-time bringing of the standards with Caesar's images into Jerusalem, and the use of temple money for an aqueduct (Antiquities 18.55–62; Jewish War 2.169–177). Tacitus says of Felix (Acts 23–24) that he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave (Histories 5.9).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/prefect-procurator
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The Gospels place the Son of God before a Roman governor, and the creed remembers it: 'suffered under Pontius Pilate'. The reference anchors salvation in real history.

John's trial scene turns the tables: Pilate asks 'Are you a king?' and 'What is truth?', while Truth stands in front of him (John 18:33–38). 'You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above' (19:11). Jesus is not a victim of Rome's power but the Lord who freely gives himself, exposing that power as it condemns the innocent.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/tetrarch
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus reports Augustus' settlement of Herod's will: Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea; Philip tetrarch of the territories north-east of the Sea of Galilee (Antiquities book 17, on the division of Herod's kingdom). Luke 3:1 lists Herod and Philip as tetrarchs, along with Lysanias of Abilene.

Josephus independently records that Antipas imprisoned and executed John the Baptist at the fortress of Machaerus, fearing his influence on the people (Antiquities 18.116–119).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/tetrarch
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Antipas is the ruler of Jesus' home region. Jesus calls him 'that fox' (Luke 13:32) and refuses to perform for him when he is sent to him during the trial (23:8–9). Luke notes that Herod and Pilate became friends that day (23:12): rival powers united against the Son.

Yet among the leaders of the church at Antioch is Manaen, 'brought up with Herod the tetrarch' (Acts 13:1). Grace reaches into the court of the man who killed John the Baptist.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/centurion
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Polybius describes the selection of centurions for steadiness and reliability rather than daring, and their place in the legion's organisation (Histories 6.24). Auxiliary units, which garrisoned Judea and Caesarea, also had centurions.

Mark uses the Latin loan-word *kentyriōn* (Mark 15:39, 44–45); Matthew, Luke and Acts use *hekatontarchēs*.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/centurion
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
A centurion understands authority and believes Jesus can heal with a word (Matt 8:8–10); a centurion at the cross is the first human in Mark to confess 'Truly this man was the Son of God' (Mark 15:39); the centurion Cornelius is the first Gentile household to receive the Spirit (Acts 10).

The soldiers of the occupying power are not enemies to be destroyed but people the Father is seeking. At the cross the executioner's officer sees the Father's heart in the way the Son dies.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/legion
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Polybius describes the organisation of the legion in detail (Histories 6.19–42). Tacitus lists where the legions were stationed under Tiberius, with four in Syria (Annals 4.5), and records soldiers' complaints that their pay was ten asses a day (Annals 1.17).

After AD 70 the Tenth Legion was left to garrison the ruins of Jerusalem (Josephus, Jewish War 7.1–5).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/legion
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The demon that names itself 'Legion, for we are many' (Mark 5:9) is driven into pigs and into the sea. Many readers hear an echo of the occupying army, though Mark does not spell it out. Either way, Jesus breaks a power that had chained a man among the tombs and returns him 'clothed and in his right mind' to his family (5:15, 19).

In Gethsemane Jesus says he could ask his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53). He refuses. The kingdom comes by the Son's trust in the Father, not by greater force.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/praetorian-guard
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In the Gospels the *praitōrion* is the governor's headquarters in Jerusalem where Jesus was tried and mocked (Mark 15:16; John 18:28). In Acts 23:35 Paul is held in 'Herod's praetorium' at Caesarea.

In Rome the praetorian cohorts guarded the emperor. Tacitus records that Sejanus concentrated them in a single camp by the city (Annals 4.2).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/praetorian-guard
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul writes from chains that the gospel has become known 'throughout the whole praetorium' (Phil 1:13), and sends greetings from 'those of Caesar's household' (4:22). The soldiers guarding him and the slaves and freedmen of the imperial service hear about another Lord.

The chain becomes a channel. Love that does not retaliate makes its way into the very structures that imprison it.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/praetorian-guard
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Where was Paul when he wrote Philippians? The traditional answer is Rome (Acts 28), which fits 'praetorium' and 'Caesar's household'. Others propose Ephesus or Caesarea, where there were also governors' praetoria and members of the imperial household (slaves and freedmen in the provinces). The choice affects the letter's date.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/crucifixion
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Cicero calls it 'the most cruel and disgusting penalty' (Against Verres 2.5.165) and says the very word 'cross' should be kept far from a Roman citizen's body, thoughts, eyes and ears (For Rabirius 16).

Rome used it to terrorise: after Herod's death the governor Varus crucified two thousand rebels (Josephus, Antiquities 17.295); during the siege of Jerusalem Titus crucified so many that there was no room for the crosses (Jewish War 5.446–451). Tacitus says Nero had Christians crucified or burned after the fire of Rome (Annals 15.44).

In Jewish tradition Deut 21:23 declared anyone hanged on a tree cursed, which Paul cites in Gal 3:13.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/crucifixion
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The cross was the empire's tool for saying who did not count. God took that tool and made it the place where his love is most fully shown. Jesus is perfect theology even here: the Father is not punishing the Son but is 'in Christ reconciling the world to himself' (2 Cor 5:19), bearing our violence rather than returning it.

In Christus Victor terms the cross is a triumph: 'he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in it' (Col 2:15). The powers that crucified him are exposed as unjust, sin and death are undone from inside, and the shamed are given the Son's place.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/titulus
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Suetonius describes Caligula having a slave paraded among guests with a placard declaring the reason for his punishment (Caligula 32). Displaying the charge was part of making an example.

All four Gospels report Jesus' charge: 'the King of the Jews'. John adds that it was written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, and that Pilate refused to change it (John 19:19–22).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/titulus
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The placard meant to mock tells the truth. The charge sheet becomes a proclamation in the three languages of the world: here is the King.

The kingship it names is the one Jesus has defined all along: he reigns by giving himself. The cross is his throne, and the first subject he welcomes is a crucified criminal (Luke 23:42–43).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/tribute-census
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Augustus records his censuses of Roman citizens (Res Gestae 8). When Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, Quirinius, governor of Syria, conducted a census of property there. Judas the Galilean urged resistance, calling payment of tribute slavery (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1–10; Jewish War 2.117–118; compare Acts 5:37).

Tacitus notes that in AD 17 Syria and Judea, exhausted by their burdens, petitioned for a reduction of tribute (Annals 2.42).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/tribute-census
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Asked whether to pay the tribute, Jesus asks for a coin and whose image is on it. 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17). The coin bears Caesar's image; human beings bear God's (Gen 1:27). Caesar may have the coin; the Father claims the person.

Jesus neither joins the revolt of Judas nor blesses the empire. He points beyond both to the relationship of image and Father that no tax can touch.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/tribute-census
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **The census of Luke 2:2.** Luke dates Jesus' birth under Herod the Great (Luke 1:5) and to a census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'. Josephus places Quirinius' census in AD 6, about ten years after Herod's death. Proposals include: Luke has confused the two; *prōtē* means 'before' Quirinius was governor; Quirinius held an earlier command in the region; or an earlier empire-wide registration is in view. No solution commands general agreement.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/publicani
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Cicero lists the trades of tax collectors and moneylenders among those that are disliked and unworthy of a gentleman (On Duties 1.150). Tacitus reports that so many complaints were made about the greed of the *publicani* that Nero considered abolishing indirect taxes altogether (Annals 13.50–51).

In Galilee and Judea, tolls on goods were farmed out by Herodian or Roman authorities; men like Levi at his toll booth (Mark 2:14) and Zacchaeus, a chief toll collector at Jericho (Luke 19:2), worked within this system.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/publicani
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus was known as 'a friend of tax collectors and sinners' (Matt 11:19). He calls Levi, eats in his house and invites himself to Zacchaeus' home before Zacchaeus has changed anything (Luke 19:5). The welcome comes first; the change follows.

Zacchaeus' restitution (19:8) shows restorative justice in action: the Father's welcome turns an extortioner into a restorer. 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost' (19:10).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/denarius
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In Matt 20:2 the landowner agrees to pay vineyard workers a denarius for the day. Tacitus records mutinous legionaries in AD 14 complaining that their pay was ten asses a day and demanding a denarius (Annals 1.17); a denarius was worth sixteen asses.

The coin Jesus asks for in the tribute question carried Caesar's portrait and inscription (Mark 12:16). Coins of Tiberius bore a title naming him son of the divine Augustus.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/denarius
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The denarius helps us feel the weight of the stories: the Samaritan leaves two days' wages for a stranger's care (Luke 10:35); the ointment poured on Jesus was worth three hundred denarii, about a year's wages (John 12:5).

In the parable of the vineyard (Matt 20:1–16) everyone receives a full day's wage. The Father's generosity is not measured by hours worked, and grumbling at it is the elder brother's mistake.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/freedman
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Gaius distinguishes the freeborn from freedmen and explains the conditions under which a freed slave became a full Roman citizen (Institutes 1.10–17).

Freedmen could become rich and powerful, especially in the emperor's household. Suetonius says Claudius gave great power to freedmen and made Felix governor of Judea (Claudius 28); Tacitus remarks that Felix used royal power with a slave's mind (Histories 5.9). Acts 6:9 mentions a 'synagogue of the Freedmen' in Jerusalem, probably descendants of Jews once enslaved and freed in Rome.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/freedman
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul plays on the freedman's double status: 'he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was free when called is Christ's slave' (1 Cor 7:22). In Christ everyone is both: set free and bound in love to the one who freed them.

Unlike the Roman freedman, the believer is not left a client with obligations but brought into the family: 'you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir' (Gal 4:7).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/doulos
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Gaius begins the law of persons with its 'principal division': all people are either free or slaves (Institutes 1.9). Slaves had no legal family and could be sold, beaten and separated from their children.

Seneca urged masters to treat slaves as fellow human beings, to eat with them and to remember that fortune could reverse their places (Moral Letters 47); his advice shows both the harshness of the system and the beginnings of criticism within it. Pliny's letter on Christians says he tortured two slave women 'who were called deaconesses' (*ministrae*) (Letters 10.96).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/doulos
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The Son 'took the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7). God comes to us at the bottom of the social order, so no one is beneath his love. In the church 'there is neither slave nor free' (Gal 3:28), and Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother' (Phlm 16).

The NT writers did not abolish slavery in law, but they planted a family logic that would undo it: a master and slave who share one Father and one table cannot remain owner and property for long. The gospel moves us from slaves to sons (Gal 4:7; John 15:15).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/lytron
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Captives taken in war could be ransomed by relatives or their city; slaves could buy or be bought into freedom. In the Torah a kinsman-redeemer could buy back a relative who had sold himself into slavery (Lev 25:47–49), and the firstborn were redeemed by a price (Num 18:15–16).

The exodus is the great redemption: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' (Exod 6:6). There God pays no one; redemption means rescue by a powerful kinsman.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/lytron
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). In context the ransom is the opposite of lording it over others: the King spends his own life to free the captives.

Read with Exodus, the ransom is about liberation from bondage to sin, death and the powers (Col 1:13–14), not a payment that changes the Father's mind. The Father is the redeemer, not the one who must be paid. This is the ransom and Christus Victor stream of the early church: the Son enters the house of the strong man and sets the prisoners free.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/lytron
blocks.body: Irenaeus describes the Word redeeming us by his own blood from the apostasy that held us captive, not by violence but by persuasion, as befits God, so that justice would not be infringed and God's ancient creation would not perish.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/lytron
blocks.body: Gregory of Nyssa explains the ransom with the image of a bait: the deity was hidden under the flesh like a hook under food, so that death, grasping at the humanity, was caught by the divinity and destroyed. He applies the ransom language to the release of humanity held captive.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/lytron
blocks.title: How the legal reading arose
blocks.body:
**How the legal reading arose.** Anselm rejected the idea that the devil had rights that God must pay off (Cur Deus Homo 1.7) and recast the problem as honour owed to God: sin is failing to render God his due, so satisfaction must be made (Cur Deus Homo 1.11–1.13). The Reformers sharpened this into penal substitution, where Christ bears the punishment justice requires.

Relational readers point out that the NT never says to whom the ransom is paid, that the background is the exodus, where God is the liberator, and that Mark 10:45 sets the ransom in the context of service, not appeasement.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/manumission
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Gaius describes the forms of manumission and the conditions, set by the laws of Augustus, under which a freed slave received full citizenship (Institutes 1.13–47).

At Delphi hundreds of inscriptions record a form in which a slave was 'sold' to the god Apollo for a price (often the slave's own savings) 'for freedom', so that the god guaranteed his liberty.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/manumission
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
'You were bought with a price' (1 Cor 6:20). The point is belonging: we are not our own, because we have been freed to belong to God. 'For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery' (Gal 5:1).

The freedom is not autonomy but family: redeemed 'so that we might receive adoption as sons' (Gal 4:5). Release leads home.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/manumission
blocks.body: Deissmann argued that the Delphic sacral manumissions, in which a slave was bought by a god 'for freedom', supplied the background for Paul's language of being bought with a price and called to freedom.

citations.ref: Light from the Ancient East (on sacral manumission at Delphi)

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/manumission
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Deissmann's sacral-manumission background is now widely questioned. In the Delphic texts the slave paid for himself and the god was a legal fiction, whereas in Paul someone else pays and the freed person belongs to the new owner. Many prefer the exodus and the ordinary slave market as background for 1 Cor 6:20 and 7:23.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/triumph
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: Suetonius describes Julius Caesar's triumphs, including a placard reading 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (Julius 37). Josephus gives an eyewitness account of the triumph of Vespasian and Titus over Judea in AD 71: the temple's treasures carried through the streets and the rebel leader Simon bar Giora led along and then executed (Jewish War 7.123–157).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/triumph
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Col 2:15 turns the image on its head. On the cross Christ 'disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in him'. The apparent victim is the victor; the powers that paraded him are the captives. This is Christus Victor in a single verse.

In 2 Cor 2:14 God 'always leads us in triumph in Christ'. Paul pictures himself in the procession, spreading the fragrance of Christ. The victory of God looks like the Son's self-giving, and those who share it are carried along in his train.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/triumph
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: In 2 Cor 2:14 is Paul one of the victorious soldiers, sharing Christ's victory, or one of the captives being led in the procession, a former enemy now displayed as God's prisoner? The Greek verb normally means to lead captives in triumph, which suggests the second; many versions translate it as 'leads us in triumph' or 'leads us as captives'. The point may be deliberately paradoxical: God's victory is shown through the weakness of his apostle.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/libation
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In the Torah a drink offering of wine accompanied the daily burnt offerings (Exod 29:40; Num 28:7). In the Greco-Roman world libations opened banquets and accompanied prayers and sacrifices; at a symposium wine was poured for the gods before drinking began.

Pliny's test for accused Christians included offering incense and wine before the emperor's image and the statues of the gods (Letters 10.96).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/libation
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul uses the image for his own life: 'even if I am being poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I rejoice' (Phil 2:17); 'I am already being poured out' (2 Tim 4:6).

This is sacrifice as self-giving love, the pattern of the Son who 'poured himself out' (Phil 2:7, *ekenōsen*). Offering is not paying God off but joining the Son's gift of himself to the Father for others.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/imperial-cult
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Suetonius says Augustus allowed temples in the provinces only if they were dedicated jointly to himself and Rome (Augustus 52). Tacitus reports that the cities of Asia voted a temple to Tiberius, Livia and the senate, and that eleven cities competed for the honour, Smyrna winning (Annals 4.15, 4.55–56); Tiberius declined a similar request from Spain (Annals 4.37–38).

Pergamum had a temple to Augustus and Rome from 29 BC. Pliny required accused Christians to invoke the gods, offer incense and wine to the emperor's image and curse Christ (Letters 10.96). The Asiarchs of Acts 19:31 were leading provincial figures associated with the provincial assembly and, many think, the imperial cult.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/imperial-cult
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The NT confession that there is 'one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 8:6) is first a declaration of love and belonging, but it could not avoid colliding with a world that asked for incense to Caesar. Revelation pictures the beast demanding worship (Rev 13) and the Lamb who was slain receiving it (Rev 5).

The contrast is not two powers of the same kind. The Lamb conquers by his blood and the faithful witness of his people (Rev 12:11), not by coercion. Worship of the Father through the Son frees people from serving any power that demands sacrifice.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/imperial-cult
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **When was Revelation written, and which emperor is in view?** The majority view dates Revelation to the reign of Domitian (about AD 95), following Irenaeus, and reads its beast against Domitian's demand for honours. Some recent scholars doubt there was a systematic Domitianic persecution. A minority dates Revelation before AD 70, under or just after Nero, and reads much of it as fulfilled in the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem (a partial-preterist reading).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/imperial-cult
blocks.body: John A. T. Robinson argued that every NT book, Revelation included, was written before the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, placing Revelation in the late 60s after Nero's persecution.

citations.ref: Redating the New Testament (chapter on Revelation)

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pax-romana
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Augustus records that the doors of the temple of Janus, closed only when there was peace throughout Roman land and sea, were closed three times under his leadership (Res Gestae 13). The Priene decree praises him for ending war.

Tacitus gives a Caledonian chieftain the famous counter-verdict: 'they make a desert and call it peace' (Agricola 30).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pax-romana
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The angels announce 'peace on earth' at a birth in the reign of Augustus (Luke 2:14). It is a different peace: not imposed by the sword but made by the Son's self-giving, 'making peace by the blood of his cross' (Col 1:20).

Christ 'is our peace' who 'has broken down the dividing wall of hostility' (Eph 2:14). The Father's peace restores relationship: with God, with one another, across the deepest divisions. 'Not as the world gives do I give to you' (John 14:27).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pax-romana
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: When Paul writes 'while people are saying, "Peace and security" (*eirēnē kai asphaleia*), then sudden destruction will come' (1 Thess 5:3), some scholars hear an allusion to Roman slogans of *pax et securitas*. Others think the phrase comes from the prophets' warnings against false peace (Jer 6:14; Ezek 13:10) and need not be political.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/caesar
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Suetonius wrote biographies of the first twelve Caesars, from Julius to Domitian. He reports that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly making disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus' (Claudius 25.4), which many link to Acts 18:2, where Aquila and Priscilla have left Rome because Claudius ordered all Jews to leave.

Tacitus records that the founder of the Christians, Christus, was executed in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/caesar
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
'Render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's' (Mark 12:17) is not a division of life into two equal kingdoms. Everything belongs to the Father; Caesar's claim is limited and temporary.

The Gospels set the story of the Son inside the reigns of Caesars on purpose (Luke 2:1; 3:1). History's real centre is not Rome but a child in Bethlehem and a man on a cross. The Caesars are named; the kingdom outlasts them.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/caesar
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Does Suetonius' 'Chrestus' mean Christ? Many think so: disputes in Rome's synagogues over Jesus as Messiah led to the expulsion. Others note that Chrestus was a common slave name and that Suetonius may refer to an otherwise unknown agitator. The date of the expulsion (often put at AD 49) is also debated.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/herodians
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: No ancient source outside the Gospels describes a party called 'Herodians'. The name follows a common pattern for partisans of a leader (as 'Caesarians' or 'Pompeians'). Josephus describes the Herodian dynasty in detail and the influence of its supporters, but not a group by this name.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/herodians
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
That Pharisees and Herodians, who had little in common, joined forces against Jesus (Mark 3:6) shows how his kingdom unsettled every faction. He healed a man on the sabbath, and the result was a plot.

Jesus does not belong to any party's agenda. He exposes the self-interest of each and calls all of them, collaborators and purists alike, to the Father's table.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/herodians
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Who were the Herodians? Suggestions include officials of Antipas' court, supporters of a restored Herodian kingship over Judea, or a loose description of anyone favouring Herodian (and so pro-Roman) rule. Some early Christian writers even described them as people who took Herod for the Messiah, but this is generally regarded as a later guess.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/sanhedrin
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus tells how the young Herod was summoned before the *synedrion* in Jerusalem for executing bandits without trial (Antiquities 14.168–176), and how the high priest Ananus convened a *synedrion* in AD 62 to condemn James, 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ', in the interval between governors (Antiquities 20.200).

The NT shows the council examining Jesus (Mark 14:55), Peter and John (Acts 4), and Paul (Acts 23), with Pharisees and Sadducees both represented (Acts 23:6).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/sanhedrin
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The council that condemns Jesus is not a picture of 'the Jews' as a whole. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus are members (Mark 15:43; John 7:50), and Gamaliel counsels caution (Acts 5:34–39). The Gospels show leaders protecting their place: 'it is better that one man should die for the people' (John 11:50).

God turns that logic around. Caiaphas' scapegoating words become, in John's telling, a prophecy that Jesus would gather into one the scattered children of God (11:51–52). The Father brings reconciliation out of the very act meant to exclude.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/sanhedrin
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: How reliable is the Mishnah's later description of a formal Sanhedrin of seventy-one with strict trial rules? Some scholars use it to argue that Jesus' trial broke many rules (night session, festival eve, quick verdict). Others think the Mishnah describes an idealised rabbinic court from after AD 70 and that the first-century council was a looser body called by the high priest, as Josephus' accounts suggest.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/synagogue
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus says Moses ordered the people to leave their other work every week and assemble to hear the Law and learn it thoroughly (Against Apion 2.175). Philo describes sabbath meeting places as schools of virtue where the Law is explained (On the Special Laws 2.62), and says Augustus allowed the Jews of Rome to gather in their *proseuchai* (Embassy to Gaius 156).

A Greek inscription from Jerusalem records that Theodotos, priest and synagogue leader, built the synagogue 'for the reading of the Law and teaching of the commandments' and a guest house for visitors from abroad; it is usually dated before AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/synagogue
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus opens his public ministry in a synagogue, reading Isa 61 and announcing 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:21). He is not founding a rival religion but bringing Israel's own hope to its fulfilment.

The synagogue gave the early church its pattern: gathering, reading Scripture, explaining it, praying. Paul went 'to the Jew first' in synagogue after synagogue (Acts 13–18). The Father's family grew out of Israel's household, not against it.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pharisees
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: Josephus says the Pharisees handed down to the people regulations from the tradition of the fathers that are not written in the Law of Moses, which the Sadducees rejected (Antiquities 13.297–298). He describes them as considered the most accurate interpreters of the Law, believing in fate and free will together and in the survival of the soul with reward and punishment (Jewish War 2.162–163; Antiquities 18.12–15), and as having great influence with the townspeople.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pharisees
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus' arguments with Pharisees are family arguments: they share Scripture, sabbath, resurrection hope and zeal for holiness. The disagreement is about what holiness looks like. Jesus touches lepers and eats with sinners, showing that the Father's holiness spreads outward to heal rather than withdrawing to stay pure (Mark 2:16–17).

Not all Pharisees opposed him. Nicodemus came to him (John 3), Gamaliel defended the apostles (Acts 5:34), and Paul remained, in his words, 'a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees' (Acts 23:6). The woes of Matt 23 are a prophet's lament over leaders, not a verdict on a people.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/pharisees
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: How influential were the Pharisees before AD 70? Josephus calls them very influential, but he also wrote after the war when their successors, the rabbis, were rising. Some scholars think the Gospels' picture of Pharisees in every Galilean village reflects later conflicts between church and synagogue; others think it fits a movement that taught the people and was active in towns.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/sadducees
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: Josephus says the Sadducees accept only the written regulations and reject traditions of the fathers (Antiquities 13.297–298), deny the survival of the soul and rewards after death (Antiquities 18.16–17; Jewish War 2.164–166), and are harsh in judgment (Antiquities 20.199). Acts agrees that they say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/sadducees
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus answers the Sadducees' trick question about resurrection by pointing to God's relationship with the patriarchs: 'I am the God of Abraham ... He is not God of the dead, but of the living' (Mark 12:26–27). A God who binds himself to people does not let death have the last word.

In Acts it is the Sadducean leadership that arrests the apostles for 'proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead' (Acts 4:2). Resurrection threatened a settlement built on present power; it announced the Father's new creation already begun.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/essenes
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: Josephus gives the longest description: entry after a period of probation, shared property, white garments, daily immersions, communal meals, oaths of secrecy, strict sabbath observance (Jewish War 2.119–161; Antiquities 18.18–22). Philo says they lived in villages, numbered over four thousand, avoided animal sacrifice, held all things in common and owned no slaves (Every Good Man Is Free 75–91). Pliny the Elder places a community of Essenes on the west side of the Dead Sea, living without women or money (Natural History 5.73).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/essenes
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The Essenes withdrew into the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord in purity. John the Baptist was also in the wilderness (Luke 1:80), but he came out to call everyone, soldiers and tax collectors included, to return to God.

Jesus went further: instead of a community separated by purity, he formed a family gathered by grace, sharing goods freely (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32) not as a rule of withdrawal but as the overflow of the Spirit's love.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/essenes
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: **Were the Dead Sea Scrolls community Essenes?** The majority view identifies the settlement at Qumran and the sectarian scrolls with the Essenes, given Pliny's location and many parallels with Josephus. Others think the scrolls come from a related but distinct group, or were brought from Jerusalem libraries. Claims that John the Baptist or Jesus were Essenes go beyond the evidence.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/zealots
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus traces a 'fourth philosophy' to Judas the Galilean, who in AD 6 taught that God alone is ruler and that paying tribute was slavery (Antiquities 18.4–10, 18.23; Jewish War 2.118). During the revolt a faction in Jerusalem called themselves Zealots, claiming zeal for good causes (Jewish War 4.160–161).

The model of zeal was Phinehas, whose violent zeal for God was remembered (Num 25:11–13).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/zealots
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus chose Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector for the same band (Matt 10:3–4; Luke 6:15). The kingdom gathers people from opposite sides of the occupation into one family.

Paul was 'extremely zealous' and persecuted the church (Gal 1:13–14; Phil 3:6). Meeting the risen Jesus redirected his zeal from violence to love. The Father's zeal is shown in the Son who weeps over Jerusalem and refuses the sword (Luke 19:41–44; Matt 26:52).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/zealots
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Was there an organised Zealot party in Jesus' day? Many scholars think Josephus' 'Zealots' as a named faction belong to the war years (from about AD 66), so 'Simon the Zealot' may mean simply 'Simon the zealous one'. Others see continuity from Judas the Galilean through the first century.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/samaritans
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
