Josephus tells of a temple built on Mount Gerizim in the Persian or early Hellenistic period (Antiquities 11.302–347) and its destruction by the Judean ruler John Hyrcanus (Antiquities 13.254–256). He also records that under the governor Coponius some Samaritans defiled the Jerusalem temple by scattering human bones in it at Passover (Antiquities 18.29–30).

John's note that 'Jews have no dealings with Samaritans' (John 4:9) and the woman's question about the right mountain (4:20) reflect this history.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/samaritans
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus crosses the boundary on purpose. He asks a Samaritan woman for water, reveals himself to her as Messiah and says the Father is seeking worshippers 'in spirit and truth', not on this mountain or that (John 4:21–24). Her town confesses him 'Saviour of the world' (4:42).

The hero of his most famous parable is a Samaritan (Luke 10:33), and the only healed leper who returns to give thanks is a Samaritan (17:16). The Father's family is bigger than our hostilities.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/diaspora
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus quotes the geographer Strabo: it is hard to find a place in the inhabited world that has not received this nation (Antiquities 14.115). Philo says no fewer than a million Jews lived in Egypt (Against Flaccus 43) and describes Jerusalem as the mother city of colonies sent out across many lands (Embassy to Gaius 281–282).

Acts 2:9–11 lists pilgrims at Pentecost from Parthia to Rome.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/diaspora
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The diaspora synagogues were the network along which the gospel first travelled (Acts 13–18). God used Israel's scattering to prepare a road for the good news to reach the nations.

James and Peter address the church as a diaspora (Jas 1:1; 1 Pet 1:1): God's family living as resident aliens in many cities, held together not by a land but by a Father and a shared hope.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/god-fearers
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body: Josephus says the temple's wealth had been increased by Jews throughout the world and by 'those who worshipped God' (*sebomenōn ton theon*) from Asia and Europe (Antiquities 14.110). He says the Jews of Antioch constantly attracted many Greeks to their worship and made them in some way part of themselves (Jewish War 7.45), and that many Greeks observe the sabbath and Jewish customs (Against Apion 2.282).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/god-fearers
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Cornelius is 'a devout man who feared God with all his household' (Acts 10:2), and Lydia is 'a worshipper of God' whose heart the Lord opened (16:14). These people stood on the threshold of Israel's house.

The gospel told them the door was open: 'God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him' (Acts 10:34–35). Through the Son they were brought fully into the family, without first becoming Jews.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/god-fearers
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Were the God-fearers a recognised category or Luke's literary device? Some scholars argued that the term never had a technical sense and that Luke created the group to bridge Jews and Gentiles. Josephus' remarks and later inscriptions listing *theosebeis* alongside Jews and proselytes have persuaded most that such sympathisers did exist, though the terms were not fixed.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/proselyte
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Josephus tells of the royal house of Adiabene: Queen Helena and King Izates embraced Jewish customs, and Izates debated with Jewish teachers whether he needed to be circumcised, one saying he could worship God without it, another insisting the Law required it (Antiquities 20.34–48).

Tacitus complains that those who convert to Jewish ways learn to despise the gods, renounce their country and disregard parents, children and brothers (Histories 5.5).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/proselyte
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Nicolaus, 'a proselyte of Antioch', is among the seven chosen to serve the church (Acts 6:5). Converts to Israel's God were welcomed into leadership.

The Galatian controversy asked whether Gentile believers had to become proselytes to belong. Paul's answer: in Christ circumcision and uncircumcision count for nothing, 'but faith working through love' (Gal 5:6). The Spirit of the Son, crying Abba, is the mark of the family.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/jubilee-debt
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Lev 25 sets out the Jubilee: 'proclaim liberty throughout the land' (25:10), each family returning to its land. Deut 15:1–2 commands a release of debts every seven years. The LXX renders these releases with *aphesis*.

Josephus summarises the Jubilee laws, including the return of land (Antiquities 3.280–286). The Mishnah attributes to Hillel the *prosbul*, a legal device allowing loans to be collected despite the seventh-year release, because people had stopped lending as the year approached (Mishnah Shebiit 10:3–4).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/jubilee-debt
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Jesus' first sermon in Luke reads Isa 61: 'to proclaim release (*aphesis*) to the captives ... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour' (Luke 4:18–19). Forgiveness in the NT carries this Jubilee freight: not only a cancelled record but restored relationships, returned inheritances, freed people.

'Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matt 6:12) makes the Father's release a pattern for community life. The kingdom is restorative justice: the Father sets things right by setting people free.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/jubilee-debt
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Was the Jubilee ever practised? There is little evidence that land was regularly returned every fifty years, and many scholars think it remained an ideal. The sabbath-year release was observed in some form (hence Hillel's *prosbul*). Whether Jesus announced an actual Jubilee year in Luke 4, or used Jubilee as an image for the messianic age, is debated.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/gymnasium
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In 175 BC the high priest Jason obtained permission to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem and enrol its people as citizens of Antioch; the priests neglected the altar to take part in the games (2 Macc 4:9–15). 1 Macc 1:14–15 adds that some removed the marks of circumcision. Josephus records the same Hellenizing move (Antiquities 12.241).

Athletes trained naked (*gymnos*), and the gymnasium was associated with the gods Hermes and Heracles.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/gymnasium
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The NT borrows athletic images freely: 'train (*gymnaze*) yourself for godliness' (1 Tim 4:7); 'run so as to win' (1 Cor 9:24); 'let us run with endurance ... looking to Jesus' (Heb 12:1–2). But it changes the goal: not civic glory but likeness to Christ.

The Father's 'discipline' (Heb 12:5–11) is the training of sons, not punishment from an enemy. 'He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.' Training is relational: a Father forming his children.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/symposium
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Pliny describes a dinner where the host served fine food and wine to himself and a few, cheaper fare to lesser friends, and the cheapest to freedmen; Pliny says he serves everyone the same, because he invites them to dine, not to be graded (Letters 2.6).

Jesus' guests reclined: a woman can stand behind him at his feet (Luke 7:38), and the beloved disciple reclines next to him (John 13:23). Mark 6:39 says the five thousand sat down 'in groups' (*symposia symposia*), literally like dinner parties.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/symposium
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Meals were where the ancient world displayed who counted. Jesus used them to show the Father's welcome: he ate with tax collectors and sinners (Mark 2:15–17), told guests to take the lowest place (Luke 14:10), and told hosts to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind (14:13).

The Lord's Supper in Corinth was failing exactly where Pliny's host failed: some ate well while others went hungry (1 Cor 11:21). Paul says this is not the Lord's supper at all. The table of the Son is a family table where all share one loaf (10:17).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/hospitality
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Abraham's welcome of three strangers at Mamre, who turn out to be the Lord's messengers, became the model of hospitality (Gen 18:1–8; compare Heb 13:2). The Didache tells churches to welcome travelling apostles and prophets as the Lord, but warns that a prophet who stays more than two days or asks for money is false, and that a traveller who settles should work (Didache 11–12).

The Theodotos inscription from Jerusalem mentions a guest house for those coming from abroad.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/hospitality
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Hospitality is the gospel enacted. The Father welcomes us as strangers and makes us family (Eph 2:19); we welcome others as he welcomed us (Rom 15:7). Jesus says that whoever welcomes the least welcomes him (Matt 25:35, 40).

The word itself, *philoxenia*, means love of the stranger. In a world where outsiders were suspect, the churches became households with open doors, and that open table did much to spread the faith.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/household-codes
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Aristotle begins his Politics by dividing the household into three relationships: master and slave, husband and wife, father and children, with the free male head ruling each (Politics 1.3, 1253b). Later moralists, Jewish writers and Roman authors discussed the same pairs.

The NT codes follow the same three pairs, which made the churches look orderly to outsiders (1 Pet 2:12).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/household-codes
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
The NT codes take the familiar form and fill it with Christ. They address wives, children and slaves directly as moral persons, which Aristotle did not. They begin with mutual submission 'out of reverence for Christ' (Eph 5:21). They define the husband's headship as Christ's self-giving: 'love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her' (5:25). Fathers are told not to provoke their children (6:4), and masters that they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven, who shows no partiality (6:9).

The household is reshaped around the Son's way of using power: to serve and to give.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/household-codes
blocks.title: Scholarly debate
blocks.body: Do the household codes accommodate Roman social order or subvert it? Some read them as a defensive move to show that Christians were not a threat, with the cost falling on women and slaves. Others stress how much they change the Aristotelian pattern by addressing subordinates as equals before God and redefining the head's role as sacrificial love. Interpreters differ on how far these instructions are culturally specific.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/letters
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
The letter of the Jerusalem council begins 'The apostles and the elders, brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles ... greetings (*chairein*)' (Acts 15:23), and the tribune Claudius Lysias writes 'to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings' (23:26). James opens the same way (Jas 1:1).

Pliny's letters to Trajan show the official letter in action: he begins his query about the Christians by saying it is his custom to refer to the emperor everything he is in doubt about (Letters 10.96), and Trajan's short reply follows (10.97). Letters of recommendation were common (compare Rom 16:1–2; 2 Cor 3:1).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/letters
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul changes the standard greeting from *chairein* to *charis*, 'grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Rom 1:7). Even his letterhead announces the gospel: every relationship he writes into begins with the Father's grace.

Letters are relational documents, written to people Paul loved and longed to see. Reading them as personal communication within a family, not as abstract treatises, keeps their doctrine warm and their warnings pastoral.

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/katallage
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
In Greek diplomacy and private life *katallagē* was the restoration of peace between enemies. Paul uses it of a wife reconciled to her husband (1 Cor 7:11).

In Jewish texts of the period it is usually the offended party, God, who is asked to be reconciled to his people: 'may he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you' (2 Macc 1:5; compare 2 Macc 7:33; 8:29).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/katallage
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Paul reverses the expected direction. God is never the object of reconciliation in his letters; he is always the subject. 'All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself ... in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them' (2 Cor 5:18–19). The Father does not need to be won over; he comes to win us back.

So the apostles are ambassadors (*presbeuomen*, 5:20) sent not to negotiate terms but to plead: 'be reconciled to God'. The enmity was always on our side. Jesus, perfect theology, shows a Father running toward estranged children, and the cross is where he absorbs the hostility and makes peace (Eph 2:16).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/christianoi
blocks.title: Historical background
blocks.body:
Tacitus says that after the fire of Rome in AD 64 Nero blamed a group hated for their vices, 'whom the crowd called Christians', named after Christus, who had been executed under Tiberius by Pontius Pilate; they were torn by dogs, crucified or burned (Annals 15.44). Suetonius lists among Nero's measures punishments inflicted on the Christians, 'a class of people given to a new and harmful superstition' (Nero 16).

About AD 112 Pliny asked Trajan whether the name itself was punishable. He reported that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day, sang a hymn to Christ 'as to a god', bound themselves by oath not to steal or commit adultery, and later shared an ordinary meal (Letters 10.96). Trajan replied that they were not to be sought out, but punished if accused and they refused to recant (10.97).

blocks.subject: entry:roman_term/christianoi
blocks.title: Reading it relationally
blocks.body:
Outsiders named the believers after the one they loved and followed. 'If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name' (1 Pet 4:16).

Pliny's report, written by an opponent, shows what Christians looked like from outside: they sang to Christ as to God, pledged themselves to honest lives, and ate together. The family of the Father was recognisable by its worship of the Son and its shared life, and that is still the best apologetic.
